title: Masahiro Sakurai's Creative Works
principle: Sum up your game in one line: its audience or hook
why: Inferred from the episode's format, not stated: every work is captioned with one line naming who it is for ('tailor-made for newcomers', 'beginners and pros alike') or its signature mechanic ('copy enemy abilities', 'smash foes off the screen').
how: Write a one-sentence pitch naming your target player or core hook and check it reads clearly as a caption.
example: Kirby's Adventure caption: 'A fun romp for beginners and pros alike that introduced the power to copy enemy abilities.'
quote: A fun romp for beginners and pros alike that introduced the power to copy enemy abilities.

title: Kirby's Adventure
principle: Make novice-friendly extras optional and skippable
why: He added three one-button minigames for novice players, with entrances on the world map so players free to skip them could.
how: Put extras aimed at one audience behind optional entrances on the map rather than in the critical path.
anti_pattern: Forcing extras on players who aren't interested.
example: Kirby's Adventure one-button minigames.
quote: All the fun, none of the complex controls.

title: Just Let Them Play!
principle: Make the fun clear within the first three minutes
why: From the arcade world: players quickly judge whether a game is fun, and if you make them wait too long they may put it down.
how: Time your opening so a new player is playing and understands the core fun within three minutes.
anti_pattern: Slow starts.
example: Arcade games.
quote: Players should understand why a game is fun in the first three minutes.

title: Just Let Them Play!
principle: Open on gameplay, not long prologues
why: Long prologues just delay players from playing; even RPGs that need introduction should lay things out so gameplay comes first.
how: Start with a playable slice from later in the story, or a battle as non-protagonist characters, and save story setup for later.
anti_pattern: Opening with long prologues.
quote: A game that starts slow is often a game that's starting on the wrong foot.

title: Just Let Them Play!
principle: Weave fun tutorials into the main game
why: Video is something other media can do, so give players a taste of the fun only games offer; tutorials should be fun too.
how: Integrate teaching into real play instead of separate, obvious practice sessions.
anti_pattern: Tutorials that feel like obvious practice.
quote: Tutorials should be fun, too. Don't make them obvious practice, but instead try to weave them more naturally into the main game.

title: Kirby Super Star
principle: Deliver volume as short, distinct scenarios to avoid fatigue
why: Too many games took too long to beat; an omnibus of quick-to-beat scenarios, each with its own gameplay, gives lots of content without tiring players of one style.
how: Split content into short, self-contained modes with their own rules and themes, chosen from a hub, and keep each one distinct.
anti_pattern: Scenarios that play the same, like Spring Breeze once copy abilities were added.
example: Kirby Super Star omnibus cork board.
quote: I thought I could provide a lot of content without causing players to grow tired of any one style.

title: Keeping Rewards in Sight
principle: Always keep a clear, reachable objective in front of players
why: Keeping rewards in sight and providing a clear objective both motivate players; it's a shame when a game doesn't keep you thinking about the next reward.
how: Check at points throughout a playthrough what the player is working toward, and add nearer objectives where it's unclear.
quote: I do think it's a shame when a game doesn't keep you thinking about the next reward.

title: Fun Beyond Game Essence
principle: Use story and characters to drive players onward into risk.
why: Stories aren't game essence but enhance it: they push players forward to face risks, and fleshed-out characters create a visceral connection.
how: Tie story beats to the challenges ahead, and design stories that use interactivity rather than copying novels or films.
anti_pattern: Relying on story alone without interactivity.
quote: They're a driving force that keeps players pushing onward to face risks.

title: Super Smash Bros.
principle: Prototype the core rules first, and pick the concept you can finish.
why: Prototypes of both concepts won praise from Nintendo; when the team urgently needed a finished game, the fighter could ship far sooner than the two-year RC game.
how: Build a bare prototype with only the core rules, and estimate each concept's development time before choosing what to make.
example: The Dragon King: The Fighting Game prototype.
quote: There were no special moves, dodges, or even items yet, but the game's rules were basically the same as Smash Bros., as you can see.

title: Spec Changes
principle: Plan for fun from the start so fun never forces a spec change.
why: Spec changes scrap finished work, cost money and hurt morale; changing course because the game isn't fun is the one to avoid.
how: Validate the core fun during planning, before committing production work to it.
anti_pattern: Discovering mid-production that the game isn't fun.
quote: What you really want to avoid is having to change course because your game's not fun.

title: Spec Changes
principle: Don't try to spec the entire finished game before building.
why: Some things only become clear once you make the game, and full up-front documentation can take as long as development itself.
how: Spec enough to start, then refine details as implementation reveals them.
anti_pattern: Writing documentation for the whole finished game from the get-go.

title: Writing Game Proposals
principle: Use one image and two lines of text per proposal page.
why: Single-topic pages read quickly like comic panels, so even a 200-plus-page deck doesn't take long to present.
how: Build each slide around one screenshot or diagram and two lines of text, with one topic per slide.
example: The Super Smash Bros. Ultimate proposal (200+ pages).
quote: One screenshot or diagram, and just two lines of text.

title: Writing Game Proposals
principle: Organize proposals into categories so listeners know where they are.
why: People can follow along and see how far into the presentation they are, and nobody likes an endless presentation.
how: Group slides into categories and subcategories with clear section markers.
anti_pattern: A long deck with no visible structure.
quote: Nobody likes an endless presentation, after all.

title: Super Smash Bros. Melee
principle: Use collectibles to include franchise characters you can't make playable.
why: There was a limit to how many fighters fit, but trophies brought other Nintendo characters in, with background info as fan service.
how: Add a collection with short background entries for characters who didn't make the playable roster.
example: Melee's Trophy system.
quote: There was a limit to how many fighters we could include in the game, but this gave us a way to bring together other characters from across Nintendo's history

title: Prep Your Proposals Hot and Fast
principle: Keep proposals brief, illustrated, and limited to what's needed
why: Keeping things interesting is key, and you wouldn't explain your grand vision to players either; what matters is the right amount of information on each page.
how: Use short sentences and images or photos to reinforce the text; cut graphs, research and the plan B; judge each page's information content rather than the page count.
anti_pattern: Lingering on the grand vision, or assuming fewer pages is better.
quote: Include only what you need, and present it as simply as you can.

title: Prep Your Proposals Hot and Fast
principle: Don't expect the proposal to hold all the fun; polish adds it
why: Proposals often lack elements that later become essential; at proposal level Monster Hunter doesn't sound novel.
how: Treat the proposal as the start and plan for polishing to be part of making the game fun.
example: Monster Hunter: hunt monsters, make gear from their materials
quote: In other words, polishing your game is also important to making it fun.

title: Kirby Air Ride
principle: Give casual players accomplishment through a progressive checklist
why: Sakurai wanted to provide a sense of accomplishment even when players are just casually playing.
how: Build an objective grid where completing one square reveals the clear conditions of the adjacent squares.
example: Kirby Air Ride's Checklist, before PS3 trophies and Xbox achievements
quote: I did this to provide a sense of accomplishment even when just casually playing the game.

title: Good Errands and Bad Errands
principle: Package errands with mystery tied to your world
why: Mechanically an errand just sets a few flags, but uninteresting tasks don't motivate; a mystery gives a sense of future developments.
how: Instead of "Go buy me some meat!", send players the same distance to look for a missing girl and investigate a house where strange noises were heard.
anti_pattern: Mundane chores and flavorless back-and-forth fetches.
example: The sick-daughter herb errand vs. the missing-girl rewrite
quote: if you're going to make players move around, there are plenty of better ways to package it.

title: Good Errands and Bad Errands
principle: Give each errand useful rewards and frequent small joys
why: Receiving things that are useful in the game, or watching an enjoyable story unfold, makes the errand worthwhile, and many pleasing moments keep it fulfilling.
how: Place combat drops, foraging finds or an unexpected twist along the route, and make the final reward useful in play.
quote: Within even a single errand, try to include many pleasing moments throughout the experience.

title: Good Errands and Bad Errands
principle: Let players choose between safe and risky routes
why: Players feel better when they choose the path forward themselves.
how: Offer at least a safer, longer route and a more dangerous shortcut to the objective.
quote: They'll feel better if they choose the path forward for themselves.

title: Good Errands and Bad Errands
principle: Skip the trip home once the objective is done
why: As with travel, the journey home isn't as exciting as the journey there; let players focus on the parts that are actually fun.
how: Whisk players back to town automatically, or offer an instant return, after the objective is completed.
anti_pattern: Making players trek back after finishing the task.
quote: I'd say it's better to let players focus on the parts that are actually fun.

title: Put Parameters in Brackets
principle: Mark parameters in specs with plain-language brackets and a placeholder
why: Specs must state clearly which parts become parameters, and each parameter's meaning must be crystal clear because several people will tune them; terse names leave room for misinterpretation.
how: Write e.g. "Initiate movement at [Special startup X-velocity is O]", rule that anything in brackets becomes a parameter, and keep a list file pairing each phrase with its value. Use it for unique specs, not global values.
anti_pattern: Naming parameters only with terse labels like "X-velocity".
example: "At the same time, decelerate by [Special X-deceleration is O/frame]."
quote: I established a rule that anything inside brackets is turned into a parameter.

title: Competing with the Past
principle: Offer something fresh that players can't find elsewhere
why: Markets are crowded because many creators keep entering them, so standing out requires something that can't be found in other works.
how: In your pitch, state what your game offers that no existing game or other medium does, and protect that during development.
quote: If you really want to stand out from the crowd, you need to offer something fresh that can't be found elsewhere.

title: Say No to Slow!
principle: Measure and maximize the time the player is in control
why: Games are full of fun experiences and making players wait to reach them is really bad; every second without fun is something to feel bad about.
how: Time a session and split it into in-control, not-in-control and empty time, then set targets to shrink the last two.
anti_pattern: Long stretches with nothing to do.
quote: When I'm making a game, I pay attention to actual playtime— the amount of time the player has control.

title: Say No to Slow!
principle: Trim cutscenes that are needless downtime
why: Cutscenes can serve as a palate cleanser, which beats keeping players busy constantly, but leaner cutscenes fit modern games better.
how: Review each cutscene: keep those that give a deliberate breather and shorten or cut those that only delay play.
anti_pattern: Relying on slowness to build suspense, which may not land today.
quote: Leaner cutscenes tend to be a better fit for games nowadays.

title: Meteos
principle: Change the core concept, not just the name of the action
why: Bombs that destroy everything already existed, and calling clears 'vaporized' or 'demolished' wouldn't make the game new.
how: Check whether a new idea changes what the player actually does; if it only renames the genre's verb, keep iterating.
anti_pattern: Cosmetic novelty that reuses the standard clear action.
example: Meteos's launch mechanic enabled secondary ignitions and air docking.
quote: Whether blocks were "vaporized" or "demolished"— the wording itself wasn't the issue. I had to change the core concept.

title: Do Competitive Games Have to Be Complex?
principle: Re-examine inherited genre rules at the start of every project
why: Genres with a long history accumulate complicated rules that don't add push and pull, and creators take familiar features for granted.
how: At kickoff, list conventions inherited from the genre or your last game and decide whether each still earns its place.
anti_pattern: Treating genre conventions as fixed givens.
example: Every Super Smash Bros. has slightly different jump mechanics because he re-examines them.
quote: To some extent, there's no avoiding complexity in games— but it's best to always approach your "givens" as if they aren't givens at all.

title: Units of Speed
principle: Specify a unit for every speed in specs and parameters
why: You can't get far in specs or parameters if you can't convey speed, so the whole team must share units of measurement.
how: Choose a project unit (px/frame for sprites, km/h or m/frame for real-scale 3D), document it and include it in every parameter name.
anti_pattern: Unitless speed values, or reusing values across hardware with different pixel counts.
example: NES, Game Boy and Super NES canvases differed, so equal speed values gave different results.
quote: So, it's essential you get your whole team on the same page when it comes to distances by specifying your units of measurement.

title: Making Tutorials Feel Natural
principle: Teach controls through real challenges, not dummy practice stages
why: Players who get straight into the game and learn by overcoming real challenges are more engaged and excited.
how: Replace separate training stages with early real obstacles that require the action being taught.
anti_pattern: Forced practice stages against dummy opponents.
example: Donkey Kong Country 3 spells out buttons with bananas in an early stage.
quote: When introducing a game, it's better to give players real challenges to face, then let them learn by overcoming said challenges.

title: Making Tutorials Feel Natural
principle: Teach movement skills in a small area that requires the skill to exit
why: Many games confine players to a small area and make them use the new movement skill to progress, teaching it inside the game's flow.
how: Build a compact enclosed space whose only exit needs the new skill, placed right after the player acquires it.
quote: For movement-based skills, many games will confine players to a small area, then make them use the skill to progress.

title: Making Tutorials Feel Natural
principle: Weave tutorials into progression so they never slow the opening
why: Any method works if players learn the controls, but tutorials that feel like work or slow down the start hurt the game.
how: Teach each mechanic at the point progression first needs it; weigh skill-preview modes against their labor and load times.
anti_pattern: Skill-preview features whose load times deter players from using them.
quote: Tutorials shouldn't feel like work, or like they're slowing down the beginning of the game— instead, try to weave them into the game's progression itself.

title: Mastering Up
principle: Plan for post-release fixes; master-up may not be the end
why: With online updates you may keep chipping away at issues that slipped into the final version, so there is no clean end.
how: Reserve people and time after master-up for patching issues in the shipped version.
quote: And if you can do online updates, you might have to keep chipping away at issues that slipped into the final version.

title: Development Secrets of the Original Kirby
principle: Visualize the design concretely early so the team proceeds confidently
why: It's easier for the team to move forward confidently with concrete visuals.
how: Mock up characters at their intended size and map full movesets before full production; Kirby Super Star's Fighter moveset and Final Cutter combo survived from such early sketches.
example: Kirby Super Star prototypes made in the Famicom dev tool.
quote: Since the beginning, it's been my style with Kirby to visualize the design as clearly as possible in the early stages of the project.

title: Mountain Climbing Is More Than Just Climbing
principle: Add flat stretches: empty areas and spots to rack up gains
why: Flatter areas, like an unexpectedly empty space or a spot to rack up gains, make exploration more fun.
how: Place quiet, enemy-free zones amid dense areas and include farming spots.
quote: Measures like these are what make game exploration even more fun.

title: Super Smash Bros. Brawl
principle: Make power features unique per character to build individuality
why: A powerful attack could have been a simple item, but giving everyone a unique Final Smash boosted each character's individuality.
how: When a feature could be generic, consider a per-character version that showcases each one.
example: Super Smash Bros. Brawl: Final Smashes.
quote: since we wanted to really boost the individuality of each character, everyone got their own unique move.

title: Don't Rely on a "Plan B"
principle: Commit to one spec in proposals; drop Plan B
why: Writing "or we could do this" leaves the decision to someone else; standing by one idea shows you've really thought it through and builds experience.
how: Look at the whole picture, pick the method you think works best, and cut hypotheticals and secondary ideas from the proposal.
anti_pattern: Leaving both doors open in a proposal.
quote: But with proposals in particular, you're better off ditching Plan B entirely.

title: Don't Rely on a "Plan B"
principle: Start from the ideal spec, then course-correct for cost
why: Beginning with the ideal and adjusting afterward to maximize cost-effectiveness is more than good enough.
how: Write the ideal version first and trim only when concrete problems surface.
anti_pattern: Twisting the proposal out of shape up front for dev efficiency.
quote: There should always be an ideal spec to start, and from there you can course-correct to maximize cost effectiveness.

title: Canceled Games
principle: Cut a doomed project before the costly final stretch
why: Costs are highest toward the end (testing, marketing, the most people), and cancellation is about cutting losses.
how: Re-weigh remaining development cost against realistic expected revenue before scaling up for the end of the cycle.
anti_pattern: Pushing a project you don't believe in into its most expensive phase.
quote: Cancellation is about cutting your losses, so if you don't think you can make it, it's best to get out while you still can.

title: Game Writing is Unique
principle: Start with gameplay, not story; save details for later
why: Players nowadays won't always latch onto a story, and long cutscenes keep action players from playing.
how: Skip long prologue exposition, put players in control immediately, and brief them while they play.
anti_pattern: Long-winded background explanations in the prologue.
example: Kid Icarus: Uprising: Pit runs through a door and gameplay begins; briefings happen during play.
quote: Start with gameplay, not with story.

title: Game Writing is Unique
principle: Never let a cutscene negate a victory the player earned
why: Winning a battle only to lose in the following cutscene is frustrating; negating achievements through story causes real stress.
how: Keep the protagonist victorious in fights the player wins, and don't stage a story loss right after a player win.
anti_pattern: Story beats that undo the player's victories.
quote: Negating the player's achievements through story writing can cause some real stress.

title: Game Writing is Unique
principle: Don't remove party members the player relies on
why: Killing off or removing comrades works in other media, but in games it can throw off party balance or cost players valuable items.
how: If a companion must leave, protect party balance and the items the player invested, or reconsider the beat.
anti_pattern: Losing party members and their gear to a story event.

title: Game Writing is Unique
principle: Tell the story from the protagonist's perspective
why: Game stories generally unfold from the main character's view; lengthy backstory about comrades or villains, common in comics, often doesn't fit games.
how: Trim side-character exposition and keep story beats tied to what the player character experiences.
anti_pattern: Long backstory digressions about allies and villains.
quote: The story generally unfolds from the main character's perspective.

title: Maps Are Game Screens, Too
principle: Shape terrain to guide players around corners and into areas
why: Positioning and depicting terrain well guides players without relying on the map at all.
how: Lay out landmarks and terrain so they naturally lead players around corners and toward interesting areas; plan how vertical spaces read.
example: Subnautica's map struggles to show vertical 3D space.

title: The Fun in Picking Sides
principle: Check every region's gambling rules before shipping wager features
why: Countries regulate depictions of gambling differently, and Smash's spectator mode needed careful, repeated adjustments to comply; it's tougher than you might think.
how: Research regional rules early for any betting-like feature and budget time for several rounds of adjustment.
example: Super Smash Bros. spectator mode.

title: Kid Icarus: Uprising
principle: Open with a simpler mode before demanding the full control set
why: Starting with the TPS land battles would force beginners to learn dodging, aiming and firing at once; the rail-shooter air battle eases them in with simple shooting and quick scenery changes.
how: Begin levels or the game with a constrained version of the core action, and add free movement and dodging after.
anti_pattern: An opening that requires every control skill at once.
example: Kid Icarus: Uprising's air battles before land battles.
quote: Starting with the TPS portion would've required the player to immediately learn how to dodge, aim, and fire— which would be a lot for beginners.

title: Kid Icarus: Uprising
principle: Tell the story during gameplay instead of briefings and cutscenes
why: Uprising's story unfolds as you play, like a radio program; because air battles had to match story beats exactly, Sakurai wrote the scenario on the development side.
how: Deliver story as in-play dialogue with an option to turn it off, and write it in-house when beats must sync with fixed-length gameplay and music.
example: Kid Icarus: Uprising's in-play dialogue.

title: The Team Behind Super Smash Bros. Brawl
principle: Use pre-production to write design docs and win stakeholder buy-in
why: Between E3 and the October start of development, Sakurai wrote the design docs and pitched each character to its original creator, so the team could begin with a plan.
how: In the gap before full staffing, finish your design documents and get approval from rights holders or key stakeholders.
example: Super Smash Bros. Brawl pre-production.

title: Super Smash Bros. for 3DS / Wii U
principle: Give each platform version a mode built on its unique hardware strength
why: A handheld means one player per screen while a home console gathers many. Linking their merits, and sharing mechanics, animations and balance, made two versions possible without double the work.
how: List each platform's distinctive quality and build an exclusive mode around it, e.g., free exploration of a huge map when every player has their own screen.
anti_pattern: Shipping two versions that differ only in raw graphical power.
example: Smash Run on 3DS (five minutes of power-up collecting on a huge map, from Kirby Air Ride's City Trial) vs. 8-Player Smash and Smash Tour on Wii U.

title: Bug Testing Never Ends
principle: Budget test hours in proportion to parameter and growth systems
why: Any game with parameters, character growth or unlockable skills is grueling to test, and a game that takes dozens of hours to finish may need thousands to tens of thousands of hours of testing.
how: When adding a stat, growth or unlock system, estimate the extra test matrix it creates and reserve QA time for it in the schedule.
anti_pattern: Adding modifier systems late without accounting for their testing cost.
example: Smash Ultimate's Spirits system made testing a gargantuan task.

title: Staying Organized with Hierarchical Outlines
principle: Write specs as a collapsible hierarchy: item, sub-item, then details
why: A folder-like outline keeps specs clean and simple, lets you reorganize items freely, and Sakurai calls it practically indispensable for keeping track of ideas.
how: Use an outline view (Word: View → Outline) with, for example, fighter name → special moves → each move's spec, collapsing the sections you aren't working on.
anti_pattern: Long flat documents that are hard to navigate or reorder.
example: A demo outline structured like Smash Ultimate's main menu. Fighter special-move specs.
quote: It's an essential tool for organizing information, and practically indispensable for keeping track of ideas— so I really can't do without it.

title: Guidelines
principle: Know which guidelines bind your game and design within them
why: Age rating, platform, storefront, online service and internal company guidelines must be strictly met or the game can't ship. When they block an intended feature, players may blame the developer without knowing their hands were tied.
how: Gather all applicable guidelines at the start and check planned visuals and features against them before production.
anti_pattern: Discovering a guideline conflict after the feature is built.

title: Guidelines
principle: Write guidelines with a clear purpose and room for leniency
why: Whether or not a guideline exists, people make the decisions, and sometimes guidelines fit and sometimes they don't. The goal is to end up with something good.
how: When you author rules for a franchise or team, state why each exists and allow justified exceptions.
anti_pattern: Enforcing guidelines rigidly where they clearly don't fit.
example: Tetris allows some exceptions for arcade games where profitability can be an issue.
quote: I think if possible, guidelines should allow for a little leniency.

title: Planning Your Game’s Rewards
principle: Design reward systems during the planning stage
why: You must reward players, but that's impossible if you have nothing to give them. A game without rewards or new developments is drab.
how: In the planning doc, list every reward type and when it arrives, and add systems if the list is thin.
anti_pattern: Bolting rewards on late in development.
quote: Hence, we should be thinking about compensation right from a game's planning and design stages.

title: Planning Your Game’s Rewards
principle: Match reward type to concept; avoid stat growth in fighting games
why: Getting stronger is the most effective reward, but in a fighting game where characters grow stronger, the "real" game seems to start only at max level.
how: If growth would undermine competition, reward with unlocks (e.g., fighters earned by beating incoming challengers), collectibles and options instead.
anti_pattern: Character-strengthening progression in a game whose fun depends on a fixed baseline.
example: Smash Bros.: fighter unlocks via challengers, coins with no stronger gear to buy.

title: Planning Your Game’s Rewards
principle: Choose collectible formats by production cost so content can scale
why: Trophies needed models and descriptions and inflated production costs. Stickers and spirits needed neither, so far more characters could be included.
how: Prefer lightweight formats (images plus a gameplay effect) when you want large collections.
anti_pattern: Making every collectible a fully modeled, written item when volume matters.
example: Smash trophies (Melee to 3DS/Wii U) vs. stickers (Brawl) and spirits.

title: Planning Your Game’s Rewards
principle: Use a goal grid that reveals neighboring objectives as each clears
why: Objectives are rewards in their own right. The grid gives players things to work toward, more than the rewards themselves.
how: Lay out conditions as panels; clearing one breaks it and shows the unlock conditions of adjacent panels.
anti_pattern: Going overboard with reward systems.
example: Kirby Air Ride's Checklist, later Smash's Challenges, predating console achievement systems.
quote: You could say that game objectives are rewards in their own right, and that motivation and reward are simply two sides of the same coin.

title: Super Smash Bros. Ultimate
principle: Build solo modes from your game's existing strengths when budgets are tight
why: A Subspace Emissary-style mode and Trophies were too costly at Ultimate's scale, so Spirits reused Smash's borrowed characters, worlds and sounds to recreate situations, with World of Light tying the battles together.
how: Design solo content around assets you already have; let players over-power themselves as a chosen difficulty, but give fewer rewards when they do.
anti_pattern: Solo content that's just one versus battle after another.
example: Super Smash Bros. Ultimate — Spirits and World of Light
quote: If you're too overpowered, though, you won't receive as many rewards.

title: Avoiding Comparison
principle: Pitch your game on its own terms, not as a copy of another
why: If your game is that analogous to another title, people may just play the original, and a company should avoid copycat accusations; only sequels should point to other games as selling points.
how: Open your proposal by describing your game's own core experience without naming another game; let listeners make comparisons themselves.
anti_pattern: Selling a new game as 'X, but with Y'.
quote: In your proposal and your final product, do your best to let things shine in a way all their own.

title: Fighter Reveal Videos
principle: Don't make shareable movies the reward for game progress
why: Brawl's per-fighter movies were meant to reward progress in Subspace Emissary, but people posted them online before release, so they stopped being much of a reward.
how: Assume in-game movies will be uploaded at launch; use them as marketing everyone can watch rather than as progression payoffs.
anti_pattern: Spending heavily on in-game movies as unlock rewards.
example: Super Smash Bros. Brawl — Subspace Emissary movies leaked via pre-release copies
quote: This meant they really weren't much of a reward.

title: Making Sequels
principle: Spend a sequel's head start on expanding the system or the content
why: Games need an underlying system, structure and tools before content can be made, so a sequel can improve that system and either expand it or get a large head start on content.
how: At sequel kickoff, list what the existing system and tools give you and decide explicitly whether the saved effort goes to system expansion or more content.
example: Super Smash Bros. for 3DS/Wii U to Ultimate — same team, similar dev environment
quote: Hence, by developing a sequel, you can improve on the existing system— and either focus on expanding it, or get a large head-start on the actual content.

title: Making Sequels
principle: Make the sequel clearly more fun and impactful than its predecessor
why: Making the same thing again roughly halves sales, and fans who see the same scale and similar content may feel they've already experienced it.
how: Write down how the sequel is more fun and more impactful than the last game, and make sure scale, content and the reveal show it.
anti_pattern: Remaking the same game at the same scale.
quote: But above all, the most vital thing is convincing players that it's more fun and impactful than its predecessor.

title: Teaching Players How to Play
principle: Teach controls inside real gameplay, never in a manual-style text wall
why: Players don't want to sit through hand-holding or read long paragraphs, and an inorganic training area just makes them want the real game.
how: Place short prompts along the path of the opening stage so players read them and immediately put them into practice; use richer hands-on methods for complex controls.
anti_pattern: Long instruction-manual paragraphs or a detached practice room.
example: Smash Bros. uses only a non-interactive video, which Sakurai considers a compromise.
quote: At any rate, I'd say it's vital that you let players play the game as you teach them.

title: Teaching Players How to Play
principle: Build modes that double as hands-on control training
why: A playable challenge teaches the controls through doing, rather than telling.
how: Design a challenge around each character's specific moves so clearing it requires using them, as Break the Targets! did.
example: Break the Targets! in the first Super Smash Bros. was designed to help players master the controls, so it's different for each character.

title: Teaching Players How to Play
principle: Schedule the hands-on tutorial as a must-ship feature
why: Hands-on tutorials for Smash were planned many times and cut, and losing the Ultimate technique mode to the schedule is a lasting regret.
how: Lock the playable tutorial into the schedule early instead of treating it as an extra that can be dropped near the end.
anti_pattern: Leaving tutorial work until late, when schedule pressure cuts it.
example: Smash Bros. Ultimate's planned hands-on technique mode was dropped for schedule reasons.
quote: I still regret that, even now.

title: It’s Easier If They Already Know
principle: Skip explanations of conventions players already know
why: Omitting or abridging what players know is a great advantage, though some players will be new to the genre.
how: Drop text like 'your guns need ammo'; at most show the attack-button icon when the first enemy appears, and still check onboarding with genre newcomers.
anti_pattern: Spelling out every basic genre rule.
example: Few FPS games tell you to fire with R2 or throw a grenade with L1.

title: Customization Lets Your Imagination Play
principle: Give every option clear pros and cons that make it distinct
why: Options with meaningful, markedly distinct differences set a game's customization apart.
how: Design trade-offs such as wide spread with short range versus narrow spread with long range, and state both sides.
anti_pattern: Options that differ in name only.
example: Wide-spread short-range weapon vs. narrow long-range weapon.

title: Customization Lets Your Imagination Play
principle: Let players test customizations immediately and make parts look cool
why: Quick testing makes changes meaningful, and nobody wants to use something that doesn't look good.
how: Allow trying a build right away, ideally swapping parts on the fly, and give every part a cool or cute design, including cosmetic-only options.

title: Staying True to Your Concept
principle: Never change your concept's direction midway through development
why: The concept is like a lighthouse; changing your trajectory gets you lost, and things only get worse from there.
how: When fatigue or doubt sets in, check decisions against the original concept instead of switching direction.
anti_pattern: Changing direction because the game isn't turning out as expected.
example: Concepts like the fun of sending opponents flying or the thrill of sprinting down a straight path.
quote: Come storm or dark of night, the one thing you should never change is your trajectory toward that light.

title: Staying True to Your Concept
principle: Don't start production until the concept is clearly in sight
why: Restarting means discarding things artists and programmers spent months on, which is costly and demotivates the team.
how: Make sure the director can state the game's appeal clearly before committing the team; amplify emergent fun rather than restarting.
anti_pattern: Moving forward without a clear concept, then scrapping work.

title: Faithfulness Comes First in Licensed Games
principle: Build on source settings that naturally map to gameplay
why: Sometimes the original setting forms the basis for a very fun game, though it still takes developer skill to add game-only ideas.
how: Find a concept in the source that works as a mechanic, then layer on systems unique to the game.
example: Megami Tensei's novel concept of summoning demons from a computer, plus the game-only idea of demon fusion.

title: Crafting “Similar” Games
principle: Give an homage many kinds of appeal the original lacks
why: The original is compelling, which is why you referenced it, so players may decide to stick with it unless yours offers more.
how: List the reasons a player would choose your game over the original and work to add many, not just one.
anti_pattern: Riding on the original's coattails.

title: Crafting “Similar” Games
principle: Compensate elsewhere when you borrow the original's systems
why: Designing the systems is the most difficult part of making games, so skipping it leaves a gap you must make up for.
how: Invest the effort saved on systems into unique appeal across other dimensions.

title: Crafting “Similar” Games
principle: Start by imitating, but finish with something unique
why: Appeal is multi-faceted and can't be measured on one scale; it's not about surpassing the original.
how: Use imitation as your starting point, and near the end of development check that your game offers what players can't get elsewhere.
quote: But by the end of development, you should strive to make something that players can't get anywhere else.

title: Making "Work" Games Fun
principle: If there's no ending, place the goal beyond the player's sight
why: Real-world tasks and profit create a synergy that keeps players from stopping, and when there is no clear ending a far-off goal keeps them going.
how: Use exponential growth or very distant milestones, as Cookie Clicker does, so players never see the finish line.
example: Cookie Clicker's exponentially growing cookie production.
quote: If your game lacks a clear ending, you might as well place it so far away that players can't even see where they're heading.

title: Using Parameters to Establish Characters
principle: Start from a neutral baseline, then push each character far from it
why: Unusable eccentricity is pointless, but characters that are basically the same are no fun; maximizing deviation from a workable neutral creates gameplay possibilities and strategy.
how: Define a neutral character for your rules, exaggerate specific parameters for each character, and iron out problems as production continues.
anti_pattern: Small, timid parameter changes, or a ship that shoots everywhere except forward.
example: Each Smash Bros. Ultimate DLC fighter has a unique system, from the Rebellion Gauge to magic cycling.
quote: Numbers are a big part of what brings characters to life! Don't just make small changes, but emphasize the differences

title: Using Parameters to Establish Characters
principle: Make each character describable in a word or two
why: Distinct traits introduce strategy and make characters memorable, the way Gordo sticks in players' memory differently from other enemies.
how: Write a one- or two-word identity for every character or enemy, and if you can't, push its traits further.
example: Gordo: invincible, never attacks, no movement pattern.
quote: In my view, characters should be made unique enough that you can describe their distinctive traits in just a word or two.

title: Using Parameters to Establish Characters
principle: Give enemies traits that gain meaning from their placement
why: Gordo alone would be an uninteresting enemy, but positioned near other enemies it gains significance in a number of ways.
how: Design some enemies as pure obstacles (invincible, harmless, static) and place them to shape how players handle the enemies around them.
example: Kirby series: Gordo placed near other enemies.
quote: If you just drop one into the game, it would make for a completely uninteresting enemy.

title: Using Parameters to Establish Characters
principle: Budget programming for each character's one-of-a-kind mechanic
why: For a character to do something no one else can, there has to be specific programming supporting it, and that cost can't be avoided.
how: Schedule engineering time per character for its unique system, such as a gauge, resource, stance switch or special input.
example: Smash Bros. Ultimate DLC: Persona, MP and Commands, Heroes' Relics, the double ARMS system, block building and more.
quote: For a character to do something no one else can, there needs to be specific programming to support that.

title: 1986: The Year of Legend
principle: Use hidden secrets for discovery, but don't punish uninformed players
why: Hidden characters and secret codes heightened the surprise and joy of discovering the unknown, but it must have been tough for players who weren't in the know.
how: Add secrets as bonuses, and make sure players can enjoy and finish the game without insider knowledge.
example: Hidden characters and secret codes popular in Japan around 1986.
quote: Though it must have been tough if you weren't in the know.

title: Mandatory Strategies and Strategic Balance
principle: Derive strategic balance from your own systems, not a reference game
why: Copying another game's approach ignores your own systems, so learn what there is to learn, then find the balance that fits your game.
how: When studying a reference game's boss design, list its lessons, then rebuild the strategy space from your own mechanics.
anti_pattern: Copying another game's strategy design wholesale.
example: Breath of the Wild feels less mandatory, perhaps because its developers rethought traditional Zelda conventions.
quote: Don't simply reference another game and craft your design based on that— learn what there is to learn, then find the balance that's right for your game's systems.

title: In-Game Cutscenes
principle: Always let players skip cutscenes, credits included
why: Even on a first playthrough it may not be the player's first time seeing the scene, and unskippable cutscenes feel off-putting.
how: Put a skip option on every cutscene and the credits from the first playthrough.
anti_pattern: Locking cutscenes until the second playthrough.
quote: On a related note, players should always be able to skip cutscenes. That includes the credits.

title: In-Game Cutscenes
principle: Add fast-forward to cutscenes, not just a skip button
why: Dialogue scenes can be skipped line by line, and people now watch videos sped up on DVRs and YouTube, so cutscenes should adapt to today's needs.
how: Let players skip ahead or fast-forward within a cutscene.

title: In-Game Cutscenes
principle: Keep cutscenes short unless they carry emotion or clarity
why: Long irrelevant cutscenes make players impatient, but cutscenes can tell a story more clearly, build emotional investment and give a breather; as rewards they lose value because they end up online.
how: Trim irrelevant scenes, reserve long ones for moments gameplay can't convey, and don't rely on cutscenes as the reward for good play.
anti_pattern: Long stretches of relatively irrelevant cutscenes.

title: In-Game Cutscenes
principle: Use quick-time events in cutscenes with extreme caution
why: Quick-time events seem to be quite unpopular, even if the aim is to keep players on edge.
how: Test any QTE with players before committing, and cut it if it frustrates them.
anti_pattern: QTEs added just to keep people on the edge of their seats.

title: Start with the Climax
principle: Open with a climactic, playable scene instead of backstory
why: Players want to take control and find out about the game, and many games start slowly with backstory, customs and relationships.
how: Put the player in control of a dramatic scene in the first minutes, and explain how things got there later.
anti_pattern: Spending a long time on backstory before letting players play.
example: Final Fantasy VII opens like the run-up to a final dungeon instead of explaining why Cloud joined Avalanche.
quote: With games in particular, players really want to take control and find out about your game— so it's no time for ambling along. Let them play, first thing!

title: Start with the Climax
principle: Show early that the enemy means business
why: A speedy start that introduces the threat immediately hooks players, while lore can be skimmed and filled in later.
how: Introduce the main antagonist within about the first minute and defer secondary details.
example: Kid Icarus: Uprising Chapter 1 throws you into an Air Battle and introduces Medusa in under a minute.

title: Start with the Climax
principle: If you can't open on a peak, keep the opening short
why: Letting events unfold through daily life is fine, but players should get control as soon as possible.
how: Shorten any everyday-life opening and hand control to the player early.
anti_pattern: A long, slow opening before the first input.
example: Phoenix Wright puts you into a trial at the very start.

title: Turning Anything Into a Competitive Game
principle: Give long games short, concrete win goals for competitive play
why: Even a slow game like Dragon Quest becomes competitive with a short goal, and moving straight to the next game keeps sessions varied.
how: Define quick objectives like "first to beat three slimes" and switch games as soon as someone wins or fails.
example: Dragon Quest: "the first to beat three slimes is the winner!"

title: Being Kind to Beginners
principle: Avoid hand-holding that makes new players feel pulled along
why: If everyone keeps telling players how to play, they feel dragged along and won't enjoy themselves.
how: Limit tutorials and prompts, and leave enough freedom for players to get into the game on their own.
anti_pattern: Constant instructions that take away the player's own discovery.
quote: You want to give them enough freedom to get into the game themselves.

title: Be Mindful of the Time Players are Giving You
principle: Treat play time as a cost to the player, not a selling point
why: Hearing a game takes hundreds of hours can make people pass on it, because they weigh that time against everything else they could be doing.
how: Don't lead marketing or design with hour counts; present the fun and let length be a by-product.
anti_pattern: Selling the game with "This game has 300 hours of content!"
quote: Play time—especially how it's perceived before starting a game— is better thought of as a cost, of sorts.

title: Be Mindful of the Time Players are Giving You
principle: Build fun first and let play time fall into place later
why: Time spent on a game should be a result of how fun it is, as when players spend hundreds or thousands of hours in Smash Bros.
how: Prioritize fun experiences and the systems that reinforce that fun before deciding how much content to make.
anti_pattern: Padding length to hit an hour target.
example: Smash Bros., which some people have played for hundreds or thousands of hours.
quote: Still, the time you spend on a game should be a result of how fun that game is!

title: Be Mindful of the Time Players are Giving You
principle: Maximize the share of time the player is in control
why: Sakurai always watches how much time the player spends in control, because the longer they're in control, the better.
how: Measure non-interactive time in a session (cutscenes, loading, menus, transitions) and cut it.
quote: That's because the longer they're in control of the game, the better.

title: Masahiro Sakurai on Creating Games: Finale Special
principle: Plan and script the entire project before production starts
why: Running the channel alongside a large game was only feasible if all content was decided in advance, and fixed categories also kept every material organized.
how: Brainstorm one-line topics, group them into categories with fixed counts, cut weak ones, outline and write everything, then lay out releases in a spreadsheet that doubles as the tracker.
anti_pattern: Improvising content as you go while juggling another big project.
example: All 256 planned episode scripts were written before recording began.
quote: In order to increase my chances of success, I absolutely had to plan all the content in advance.

title: Masahiro Sakurai on Creating Games: Finale Special
principle: Prove feasibility with a finished-quality pilot before committing
why: Sakurai made a three-episode pilot to find out whether he could really make the channel, then used it to win Nintendo's cooperation and convince his editing company.
how: Complete two or three representative pieces at final quality, use them as a go/no-go test, and show them to partners and rights holders.
example: Pilot episodes C03 "Keeping Rewards in Sight," C11 "Praise the Player!" and D03 "Jump Physics."
quote: I did this to find out whether or not I could really make this channel, and the answer was: Yes! I can do it!
